Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

#6529. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6528. Homemade Cranberry Sauce

I don’t care if you love it or hate it—cranberry sauce is a Thanksgiving STAPLE. Personally, I love it. Every year, you can find me spooning multiple helpings of the sweet-tart sauce onto my plate to balance out all of the rich savory dishes. While I understand the nostalgic appeal of the canned stuff, homemade cranberry sauce is 1,000x better. It's fresh, versatile, and so easy to make. All you need are 5 ingredients and 20 minutes to make this staple holiday side.

What People Are Saying:“This is the simplest, but tastiest cranberry sauce i’ve ever made… My family loved it so much, i’ve had to make several batches for christmas gifts, per request.” -OrangeSushi

“Made this for Thanksgiving, and everyone loved it, including the ones that don’t care for cranberry sauce!! I added some fresh mandarin oranges and cinnamon to mine. Everyone wanted leftovers to take home! We put it in our oatmeal with pecans for breakfast in the morning! I plan to make this all year round instead of just at Thanksgiving! ❤️” -RedDice

First, grab a small saucepan—but not just any saucepan! Make sure it’s either stainless steel or enameled cast-iron. Whatever you do, avoid aluminum, which will react with the copious acid in the berries, giving the sauce an unpleasant metallic taste. Add the sugar and 1 c. water and stir until the sugar is dissolved. Now add the cranberries and bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat.

The beauty of cranberries is that (1) they readily burst and release their juices, and (2) their juices have so much natural pectin that the berries thicken nearly to jam in mere minutes. Ten minutes of simmering, with some occasional stirring thrown in, is all the cooking required. Don’t sweat it if a small minority of the berries haven’t burst—they probably will by the time the sauce has cooled.

Stir in the orange zest and let the sauce cool; it will continue to thicken. And believe it or not, that really is all there is to it. What’s more, this is a Thanksgiving dish you can get off your plate up to 1 week in advance. Just transfer the cooled cranberry sauce to an airtight container and refrigerate until the big feast. Bonus: The flavors will continue to meld and deepen while it hangs out in the fridge.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

While this version is perfectly classic, if you want to experiment, you’ve got a few options. If your cranberry sauce isn’t complete without orange juice, you can sub freshly squeezed or bottled orange juice for some or all of the water. Alternatively, if you’re averse to oranges, feel free to skip the zest and add a pinch of ground cinnamon or a couple of cinnamon sticks instead. Craving some crunch? Throw in some chopped pecans at the end of cooking.

Check out our keto cranberry sauce if you're looking to satisfy every diet, or our cranberry relish if you want a similar side without having to turn on your stove.

If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.

#6525. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. So we teamed up with the brand on a 12-week collaboration. The BA Picks collection features recipes hand-selected by our staff, and HelloFresh customers also get an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit. To choose them, we cooked many, many kits in our home kitchens and in the BA Test Kitchen, following the recipe cards exactly. We judged each one on flavor, portion size, cook time, cuisine variety, and the recipe's step-by-step clarity. This Ginger Chicken and Rice Bowl is one of those picks. Here’s what it’s like to make it at home.

As a product tester, I'm very methodical, so I was excited to help build the BA Picks collection. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. Despite being Italian, I'm constantly drawn to Asian flavors when I cook at home on weeknights. The balance of salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic is highly addictive. It hits the spot after a long day of reviewing appliances in the Test Kitchen.

That's why the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls caught my eye. Made with soy, Thai chili sauce, gochujang, ponzu, and Korean chili flakes, it has all the flavors I crave. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.)

HelloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

This kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

The pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. (Always sanitize your cutting board and prep station after working with raw meat!) So HelloFresh came in clutch here. The only ingredients I had to pull from my own pantry were oil, salt, pepper, and a small dash of sugar.

HelloFresh instructions include photos of each step, so they're easy to follow. I started by putting a pot of rice on. Then I chopped and salted the cucumbers so they could season while I cooked the chicken. After a quick sauté in a pan, I tossed the chicken in the sauce, and it was ready. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

This dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

The Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. Find it in the BA Picks collection on HelloFresh, along with an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit.

#6524. Apple Fries

Here’s how to make Legoland’s legendary apple fries, complete with the cinnamon sugar coating, caramel drizzle and vanilla whipped cream dip.

Legoland’s most popular food isn’t the usual lacy funnel cake or plate of chicken tenders. Look around for the longest line, and you’ll find it at Granny’s Apple Fries, where deep-fried apple sticks are coated in cinnamon-sugar, drizzled with caramel sauce and served with vanilla whipped cream. Thankfully you don’t need to wait in line (or buy a ticket to the park) to enjoy these legendary apple fries. Here’s how to make a copycat version of Legoland’s apple fries right at home, down to the homemade whipped cream and caramel sauce drizzle.

Peel and core the apples. Using a sharp knife, carefully cut the apples into 1/2-inch sticks.

Place the cornstarch in a large bowl. Add the apple sticks, a few at a time, tossing to thoroughly coat them. Shake off the excess.

In an electric skillet or deep-fat fryer, heat the oil to 375°. Fry the apple fries, a few at a time, until they’re golden brown. Drain the oil from the apple fries by placing them on paper towels.

In a small bowl, stir together the granulated sugar and cinnamon. Immediately sprinkle the mixture over the hot fries. The sooner you sprinkle, the better the mixture sticks.

Editor’s Tip: Never, ever overcrowd your skillet or deep-fat fryer. Doing so may cause a dangerous boil-over. Always work in small batches.

In a small, chilled glass bowl, use chilled beaters to beat the heavy whipping cream until it begins to thicken. Add the confectioners’ sugar and vanilla extract, and beat until soft peaks form.

Serve the apple fries warm with the vanilla whipped cream. If desired, drizzle the apple fries with warmed caramel sauce.

Allow leftover apple fries to cool completely to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container. They can last in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze apple fries. Allow them to cool to room temperature, then transfer them to an airtight container with pieces of parchment or waxed paper between them. Freeze them for up to two months. Reheat them in a 400° oven until they’re crispy and warmed through.

To cut apples for apple fries, peel and core the apples, then cut them into fourths. From there, cut the apple into 1/2-inch slices lengthwise, then turn each slice on its side and cut it in half lengthwise. You should be left with apple matchsticks.

If your apple fries are soggy, the oil temperature was likely too low. When the oil isn’t hot enough, it will soak into the cornstarch and make it soggy rather than crisping the fries. It’s a common deep-frying mistake, so make sure to keep a close watch on the oil’s temperature.

Serve apple fries immediately while they’re still hot. We love to finish them with salted caramel sauce and dip them in the vanilla whipped cream. Serve your apple fries with hot apple cider or homemade hot chocolate to make your treat extra decadent and sweet.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

#6521. This Is the Jarred Pasta Sauce Ina Garten Always Keeps in Her Pantry

"Store-bought is fine" carries a little more weight when Ina tells you exactly which pasta sauce to buy.

I can happily spend an entire afternoon making dinner. Give me a little music, a glass of wine and something to braise, and I’ll settle in without much concern for when it all reaches the table. It’s a lovely way to cook when I have the time, but leisurely cooking isn’t always practical for busy parents. On most days, dinner needs to fit into my family’s schedule, and my kids don’t want to hear that dinner is still achieving important levels of depth and complexity as it enters its sixth hour on the stove.

But having less time to cook shouldn’t lower our expectations for dinner. A simple plate of pasta can be every bit as satisfying—provided the ingredients involved are worth eating. It’s why I’m particular about store-bought sauce. I’m happy to buy it, but I want to enjoy it as much as anything I spent time making myself.

Ina Garten seems to have arrived at a similar conclusion. Her signature “store-bought is fine” reassurance comes with some excellent recommendations, including the marinara from Rao’s Homemade, a brand I’ve been loyal to for years. It’s a small thing to have in common with Ina, but until I acquire a Parisian apartment of my own, I’ll gladly take it.

“Why make your own marinara when Rao’s marinara sauce tastes homemade?” Ina has said. It’s a reasonable question, particularly coming from someone with very little left to prove in the kitchen.

She’s equally decisive on her website. When a reader asked her favorite jarred marinara, Ina answered, “That’s easy! Rao’s Marinara Sauce.” It also appears among her recommended ingredients in the site’s shopping section.

Her advice to an incoming college student gives the recommendation some practical context. When asked which staples to have on hand, Ina suggested keeping pasta and Rao’s marinara around for a ten-minute dinner. That’s useful advice at any age, particularly once you discover that graduation doesn’t necessarily leave you with more time to cook.

Ina’s comment about homemade flavor gets at why I’ve continued to buy it, too: Rao’s has the richness and depth I want in a sauce, even when I’m serving it with nothing more elaborate than bucatini and Parmesan. I actually look forward to that dinner. The fact that it comes together quickly is just a bonus.

Lately, I’ve been especially impressed with the brand’s new creamy roasted garlic sauce (so much so that I gave it a Taste of Home Award). The mellow roasted garlic and the richness of mascarpone have made it a favorite in my house.

Ina’s explanation of “good ingredients” offers a useful starting point. In Modern Comfort Food, she writes, “They don’t have to be expensive, but they need to be chosen thoughtfully.” Her emphasis is on flavor and choosing ingredients because of what they contribute to the finished dish.

When it comes to Rao’s, she points to slow simmering and good tomatoes, basil, garlic and oregano. That makes the ingredient label a sensible place to begin when comparing jars. The marinara label lists whole peeled Italian tomatoes, followed by olive oil, onions, salt, garlic, basil, black pepper and oregano—and no added sugar.

For a classic marinara, look for that familiar foundation of tomatoes, oil, aromatics and herbs. If you prefer a more savory sauce, keep your eye on the added sugar, too. These are useful details to compare across brands, although the label can only tell you so much about how well the ingredients have been cooked and balanced. In this case, I’m happy to let Ina’s recommendation settle the matter.

#6519. The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.

My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

This habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

With the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food plan,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

The USDA established the Thrifty Food Plan in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over New York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”

However, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

Fruit cart vendors, common in New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

What if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

Whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

Note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

The TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

Last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

Shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

So I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:

Does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

Um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

Lenarczyk, M., Kronenberg, A., Kwok, A., Borg, A., Alsheikh, A. J., Mathison, A. J., Zimmermann, M. T., Lawton, S. B. R., Raff, H., Willey, J., Komorowski, R. A., Urrutia, R., & Baker, J. E. (2026). Multiple simulated spaceflight stressors impact cardiac fibrosis, calcium dynamics, immune function, cytokines and gene variants in rat, Rattus norvegicus. PLoS ONE, 21(9), e0357485. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0357485

#6515. Smash Tacos Are The Dinner Hack My Family Never Stops Requesting

Whether I’m whipping up a quick weeknight dinner for one or feeding the whole family, smash tacos are always a good call. Featuring a layer of crispy meat pressed into a soft tortilla that’s topped with condiments of your choice, they’re a speedy, flexible dinner that readily adapts to whatever you have in your fridge.

While I have tons of experience with smash dumplings, I made my very first smash tacos while developing the recipe for chicken Caesar smash tacos and coming up with the concepts for meatball sub smash tacos and Philly cheesesteak smash tacos. As I quickly learned, smash tacos are pretty simple to make, but if you haven’t done it before, there are definitely a few things to know.

Here are a few tips to make your first experience making them just a little smoother:

Whether you’re mixing in a ton of spices or keeping it simple with just salt and pepper, it’s important to work the ground meat until it feels tacky; otherwise, the meat won’t hold together on the tortilla when you sear it, and you’ll end up with a fragmented patty instead of one smooth layer.

Even if you’re using 90% lean, beef shrinks when it cooks, so if your patty is beef, spread it to the very edge of the tortilla—maybe even a little over. That gives you the best chance of getting full coverage once it’s cooked. Chicken, on the other hand, doesn’t shrink much at all (in my experience), so in that case it’s fine to leave a little border around the edges.

Let the patties sear, undisturbed, for a solid two minutes before flipping them. This gives you the best shot at that caramelized crust, and that’s where all the flavor is!

A smash taco doesn’t always require cheese (see the gyro smash tacos below!), but if you’re going there, I highly recommend using the broiler to melt it. In my experience, Kraft singles are the only type of cheese that will melt completely before the bottom of the smash taco burns. It might be an extra step, but it’s worth it to avoid an acrid bottom.

A truly amazing smash taco needs a plethora of toppings, so don’t hold back here! Load it up. While the OG smash tacos were a mash-up of a smash burger and a taco, you don’t need to limit yourself to classic burger flavors here. Almost any sandwich can be hacked into the smash taco format, but as I’ve discovered, salads are also fair game for inspiration. Here are five of my favorite smash taco flavor profiles:

Taking inspiration from the granddaddy of all burgers, these smash burger tacos feature all the familiar fixings of a classic Big Mac, including American cheese, “shrettuce,” pickles, and Big Mac sauce. All they need is a side of fries.

When you’re craving a salad, but everyone else at the table insists they need “real” dinner, these chicken Caesar smash tacos are the perfect compromise. Ground chicken patties are topped with squiggles of Caesar dressing, a mound of romaine, crispy croutons, and tons of cheese for a dinner that manages to make even a taco feel healthy.

I love ordering a cheesesteak when I’m out, but if I’m craving one at home, these Philly cheesesteak tacos are my lazy go-to. Topped with sautéed peppers and onions and lots of melty provolone cheese, they’re the perfect quick weeknight meal—or late-night snack. And, unlike an actual cheesesteak, you can definitely eat more than one!

Gyros and tacos are iconic all on their own, but now there’s actual proof that they can become something even better when they’re combined. Loaded with shawarma-spiced chicken, cucumber, tomato, tzatziki, and (of course!) shoestring fries, these gyro smash tacos are the definition of over-the-top indulgence.

Forming and baking individual meatballs can take some time, but these smash tacos are the perfect shortcut. Topped with marinara, mozz, and plenty of Parm, they’re bringing all the saucy, cheesy comfort vibes of an actual meatball sub—just in a quicker, more convenient weeknight package. Fresh basil on top is nice if you have it. If you don’t, a little dried oregano also works!

#6513. The Best Subscription Boxes for Men, Tested for Quality and Value

Tested by Emily Way, Paul Rankin and Caroline Lubinsky

From craft beer and gourmet jerky to bold coffee and unique snacks, these food and drink subscriptions are gifts any guy will love.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

When it comes to gift and subscription boxes for men, brands like Bespoke Post and Dollar Shave Club often get the spotlight. But at Taste of Home, food is our specialty, and we know a thing or two about food subscriptions. That’s why we’ve rounded up our favorite food and drink subscription boxes for men, with something for every palate, from savory jerky and craft beer to bold coffee.

We tracked down and tested some of the best food clubs to find boxes worth savoring. Whether you’re shopping for a hard-to-buy-for guy or treating yourself, these thoughtfully curated subscriptions make it easy to discover new flavors and enjoy something delicious month after month.

I’ve said it before, but if you ask my husband what his favorite part of my job is, he might say it’s when I get to test a meat delivery box. And Porter Road, essentially an online butcher shop, is one of my favorites.

The Best of Porter Road Box truly makes a fabulous gift for the meat lover in your life. With bone-in pork chops, ground beef, bacon, dry-aged steaks, breakfast sausage and chorizo links, this specific box offers a wide variety of all the brand has to offer. But Porter Road also has many other curated subscription boxes to choose from, too.

If you know (or you are) a meat lover who appreciates great-tasting cuts, it’s certainly a subscription  worth the investment. The meat I tried was flavorful, tender and high-quality, comparable to that of a local butcher shop with top quality meats.

Available every two, four, eight weeks or twelve weeks, you can choose how often your special, curated box of meat is delivered. And if you’d rather create your own custom subscription box to gift, you can do that too for a gift he’s sure to love.

Men like meat, right? If you’re looking for yet another meat subscription option, this one is bacon specific. Tester Marisa Hillman tried three months of Goldbelly’s bacon club, which offers approximately 2 to 5 pounds of bacon from a new butcher each month. Her first box, which was her favorite, came with four 14-ounce packages of bacon from The Loveless Cafe in Nashville: hickory, applewood, maplewood and peppered.

“I cooked a package of the Goldbelly bacon, immediately followed by a package of grocery store (Jimmy Dean brand) bacon,” says Marisa. “The difference was incredible. The Goldbelly bacon slices were thick and flavorful with minimal grease left behind. The grocery store bacon slices were thin and I had to empty the grease three times while cooking.”

Marisa’s second delivery was a bit more adventurous. It included two 12-ounce packages of bacon, one 8-ounce package of jowl bacon and one 8-ounce package of bacon bits from Smoking Goose in Indiana. While she didn’t love the jowl bacon, she did enjoy the bacon bits and Smoking Goose bacon.

Her third box included two 1-pound packages of regular bacon from Benton’s Smoky Mountain Country Hams. Marisa noted that the final shipment contained bacon which was mostly fat. While the fatty cuts didn’t particularly appeal to her, it may to folks who are open to non-traditional bacon—especially adventurous cuts.

With Murray’s Mac and Cheese Club, he can have fresh warm and gooey macaroni and cheese whenever. The mac and cheese arrives ready to be heated in the oven or stashed in the freezer, so a comforting meal is just moments away when the craving strikes.

You can opt for a three, six or twelve month subsctiption, and each month brings a shipment of two 32-ounce frozen mac and cheese portions. One is always Murray’s famous, classic cheddar flavor. The other is a different flavor each month that’s exclusive to the club.

“I received both a regular and spinach and artichoke mac. The mac and cheese looked good right out of the box, and both were still nicely chilled from the ice,” says tester Caroline Lubinsky. “I was a little surprised to see that they were a bit smaller than I expected for the price, but they looked appetizing in the pans.”

In comparison to other easy, cheesy brands (think Kraft or Annie’s), Murray’s definitely takes the cake. We also like that you receive a specialty flavor each month. While the packaging is more practical than it is pretty, this delicious subscription makes a great gift for someone who loves carbs.

Gourmet jerky delivered right to your door? Say less. If you have a jerky lover in your life, this is the gift for them.

Our own resident jerky lover Paul Rankin tried Jerky Dynasty Club and was impressed by everything from the presentation to the products. “I loved how much variety there was in the box, definitely plenty of jerky to get me through an entire month (or more),” he says in this Dynasty Club review.

Paul’s box contained three big bags of jerky and some smaller meat sticks. While the contents were mostly beef and pork jerky, there were also some unexpected meats like venison, elk and wild boar. In total, he received bags of Carnivore Candy Peppered Brisket jerky, Ayoba-yo Droëwors beef sticks, Smoking Gun Wicked Mary jerky and Hunters Reserve Roadkill summer sausage. He also enjoyed an Indian Valley Venison Pepper jerky stick and a Dill Pickle jerky stick. “The flavors were intense and interesting,” says Paul.

In addition to delicious jerky, Paul points out that this subscription is a great value. “Considering how much a regular bag of jerky is at the grocery store, this subscription box is a great deal,” notes Paul. “A regular bag of jerky is around $12 at my grocery store (for under 3 ounces), and this box gives you 16-24 ounces, so your dollar is really stretching far.”

The City Brew Tours club really is a club, complete with its own monthly podcast for die-hard brewski fans, making it the perfect subscription gift for hop heads.

The City Brew Tours staff curates each selection and includes a detailed printout containing information about the tasting notes and breweries chosen, plus a little about the featured city. Inclusions range from sours to IPAs and everything in between, so it’s an ideal subscription for those who appreciate beers of all kinds.

“My box arrived filled to the brim with brews from Pittsburgh. The insert with an overview of the city, facts about Pittsburgh brewing and info about each beer was incredibly enlightening and a great introduction to what the city offers,” says Shopping Editor Emily Way. “It was also cool to have access to the tasting notes and enjoy two brews from each brewery—not to mention all the one-on-one insight gleaned from the Zoom call.”

You don’t have to know the ins and outs of his home coffee setup to gift this coffee membership subscription. The Cometeer coffee subscription features the convenience of instant coffee without the taste of instant coffee. Score! These genius recyclable capsules rely on flash-frozen coffee concentrate and ship directly to your door.

“I tried several types of Cometeer coffee a while ago, and I’ve been thinking about it ever since. I can’t get over the convenience factor,” says Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski. “The pods are perfect on busy (or, let’s be honest, lazy) mornings when I don’t want to pull out my grinder and make a mess of grounds all over the countertop.”

Simply grab a pod from the freezer, mix it with hot water or milk and enjoy it as hot coffee, an iced latte or even an espresso martini. No brewing required! Moreover, Cometeer offers multiple roast options from over a dozen roasters.

And don’t forget to check out the Cometeer Advent Calendar this year as an early Christmas gift for java lovers!

If he likes to indulge in a little charcuterie every now and then, a cheese of the month club is a cool way to shake up the usual cheddar or brie boards. Of all the options we’ve tried, Murray’s reigns supreme for its cheese of the month club. Rather, its cheese of the month clubs. Our favorite is the Cheese Explorer’s Club, which contains three different cheeses from a variety of cheesemakers across the globe each month.

We love the brand’s bold, outside-the-box cheeses from domestic and global cheesemakers, and the fun facts and serving tips included in each box.

“I got three herby Vermont Creamery Goat Cheeses in the first box of the month. The second month’s box had more variety: Murray’s Gemma Di Langa, Meredith Dairy Sheep and Goat Cheese and Alisios,” says tester Caroline of her three-month subscription. Even more notably, each box arrived completely chilled.

And surely, you can’t go wrong gifting a snack club. Whether it’s savory or sweet, a box full of delicious treats is a surefire way to show your favorite foodie you care. Universal Yums is our favorite snack subscription that allows you to experience popular snacks from different countries.

In addition tasty treats, each snack delivery box also includes an illustrated map, a tasting worksheet, allergy labels and a pamphlet full of cultural facts, fun quizzes and background info on each treat. The snacks in this international snack box are genuinely sourced from their featured countries, which adds to the authenticity.

“I received the Yum Yum Belgium Box with 10 snacks,” notes product tester Annamarie Higley. “Unpacking this box made me want to pack my bags and head back to Belgium. The snacks were so authentic—every one of them was made within the country’s borders, excluding the chips, and this fact was very prominently noted.”

Universal Yums is a fun way to explore different cultures through snacks. With three box sizes to choose from, each package includes 5 to 18 snacks. You can choose a one-year subscription, pay for six months, or purchase one month at a time. To get started, pick from about 10 different destinations for your first box and enjoy a taste of somewhere new.

If you want to give the gift of snacks with a healthier twist, the monthly HealthyMe Living Snack Box is a great option. Each box includes 8 to 10 snacks carefully curated by a certified holistic health coach. Even better, the snacks feature minimal, high-quality ingredients without unnecessary fillers or artificial sweeteners.

The box arrived packed with 10 snacks wrapped in blue tissue paper, and all but one were new to registered dietitian and product tester Nancy Snyder. “From protein bars and popcorn to infused almonds and ginger chews, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and taste of each snack. I loved the variety and getting to try treats I couldn’t find at my local grocery store,” she says.

Prefer a specific diet? Choose a vegetarian or gluten-free box. Nancy found that the regular box also offers a nice mix of snacks to suit different dietary preferences.

This one is definitely an acquired taste, but seafood lovers and fans of trendy tinned fish will appreciate the Tinned Fish Club. Each month, members receive two to four premium tins of seafood, plus seasonings and pairing suggestions.

Tester Emily was impressed with the packaging and the flavors. “If you love fish and flavor, you really can’t go wrong with this box, which pairs uncommon, flavorful tinned seafood with mouthwatering seasonings, all shipped directly to your door,” she says.

Each box also includes a brochure with tasting notes, product details and pairing ideas, making it fun to discover something new. “As a big-time tuna fan, I loved receiving a tin of Santa Caterina tuna in Molho Cru sauce, along with mayo, crushed red pepper and pink sea salt to enjoy alongside,” Emily says.

For anyone who loves sardines, mussels, tuna and other seafood specialties, this subscription is a real catch!

To find the best subscription boxes for men, we considered our own extensive testing with gift clubs. Over the course of testing for other lists, we compiled our “best overall” picks to inform this piece. Our expert team of editors and product testers thoroughly tested and evaluated each option in our own homes and kitchens, and we took notes on the following aspects:

When it comes to gift and subscription boxes for men, picks from brands like Bespoke Post and Dollar Shave Club are often recommended. But at Taste of Home, food is our specialty—and we know a thing or two about food subscriptions. That’s why we’ve rounded up our favorite food and drink subscription boxes for men, with something for every taste, from savory jerky and craft beer to bold coffee.

At Taste of Home, we’ve tested countless food and drink subscriptions, informing pieces like the best food subscription boxes, gifts of the month clubs, fruit subscriptions, chocolate subscription boxes, and so many more. #6512. Taco Bell Made A Hot Dog With A Chalupa Bun & Fans Are Horrified

“Imagine getting a glizzy from Taco Bell 😭”

Taco Bell is no stranger to controversial menu items, but one new viral dish might be the wildest yet.

Last week, the Tex-Mex chain launched the first-ever Live Más Open, a star-studded golf tournament hosted by Kevin Hart. The guest list for the nine-hole competition included pro athletes, television stars, musicians, and more. However, the appearance that’s generating the most buzz isn’t a celebrity—it’s a Taco Bell hot dog.

Attendees were served a lineup of event-exclusive dishes that we've never seen at the Bell before, like lemon pepper ranch-dusted chicken nuggets and pimento cheese Quesaritos. Taco Bell fans, though, have the most FOMO for the Fire Piña Hot Dog.

According to FoodBeast, the dish featured a hot dog served with the chain’s signature chalupa flatbread instead of a traditional bun. Taco Bell loaded the hot dog with grilled pineapple, cotija, pickled red onion, cilantro, and two different sauces. The exact sauces haven't been confirmed, although one attendee suspected they might be sour cream and Taco Bell Fire Sauce.

Bailey Fink from Allrecipes attended the Live Más Open and tasted the hot dog for herself. She called it “easily one of the best hot dogs I’ve ever had” from a fast-food restaurant and compared the flavor profile to a traditional Colombian hot dog (minus the potato chips).

Social media users who didn't get the chance to try the Fire Piña Hot Dog, though, don't seem too convinced. “The words Taco Bell and hot dog should not be in the same sentence,” one Instagram user wrote. Another added, “If you order a hot dog from Taco Bell, you need to be on watch list…”

But if you take a look at Taco Bell's origin story, introducing hot dogs would actually bring the chain full circle. Founder Glen Bell's early restaurants served hamburgers and hot dogs before he shifted his attention to tacos. He eventually opened Taco Tia, which preceded the first Taco Bell restaurant in Downey, California.

Unfortunately, though, it appears Taco Bell won't be adding hot dogs to the menu anytime soon. All the dishes served at the Live Más Open were made exclusively for the event, and the chain currently has no confirmed plans to roll them out nationwide.

But don't despair: Part of the golf tournament prize is the opportunity to help choose a discontinued menu item to bring back for a limited time next year. So while a Taco Bell hot dog likely isn't in our immediate future, we can still look forward to the return of an old favorite.

#6511. In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender quickly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to plan what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

“We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke says. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”

Being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

Although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

“Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

Puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

Huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

The best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I quickly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

Although Huyke auditions new Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

Next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in New York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in New York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

Then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

Many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also shows me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

“I believe every cuisine evolves,” she says. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”

#6509. Is It Safe to Eat Raw Cranberries?

This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl. Could you eat cranberries raw if you wanted to?

Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own. The fruit is familiar enough to be indispensable at Thanksgiving, but rarely considered when we’re in the mood for a bowl of berries to snack on.

I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving. Cranberry bogs are part of the landscape, and local berries fill jars of jam and syrup at roadside stands. This fall, my family attended the annual cranberry festival, where a friend of ours was crowned Cranberry Queen. (It’s a small town.)

Even here, though, cranberries generally arrive at the table with enough sugar to soften their bite. That sharpness is welcome in a buttery loaf or in a cranberry sauce alongside a rich turkey dinner, but a plain berry is a very different experience. So is all that preparation a matter of preference, or do cranberries actually need to be cooked before you eat them?

Yes, cranberries are safe to eat raw. There’s no need to cook them first; simply rinse them under cool running water and discard any that are soft, shriveled or spoiled. What happens after that is largely between you and your tolerance for sour foods.

Raw cranberries are firm and sharply tart, with a bitterness that can get lost beneath the sugar in cranberry sauce and muffins. They’re also astringent, meaning they leave you with a dry, puckering feeling in your mouth. If you loved the sour fruit trend of adding citric acid to grapes, then you might happily eat a few plain cranberries, but their absence from the average person’s fruit salad is understandable.

They have plenty to offer nutritionally, too. One cup of raw cranberries provides about 4 grams of fiber and 13 milligrams of vitamin C, along with naturally occurring antioxidants. They’re also naturally low in sugar, though that tends to change once we start mixing them with the things that make us love them.

I like cranberries best when their tartness is balanced by something rich or sweet. In a cranberry orange bread, the berries become little pockets of sharp fruit that break up the sweetness, while orange zest and warm spices round out the flavor. They do the same for muffins, cakes and scones, where an acid bite is particularly welcome among all that butter and sugar.

Of course, making sauce remains a very good use for a bag of cranberries. Simmering softens the berries until they burst, and sweetening lets you appreciate their flavor without quite so much puckering. At Thanksgiving, that acidity is part of the appeal: A spoonful brings some relief to a plate largely devoted to gravy, cream and butter. I’m equally happy to see the fruit on the next day’s turkey sandwich along with plenty of mayonnaise.

If you’d rather leave the berries uncooked, chopping them finely makes their intensity easier to distribute throughout a dish. A fresh relish with orange and sugar preserves their crisp texture, while cranberry salsa takes them in a savory direction. You can also blend a small handful into a smoothie with sweeter fruit.

And if you bought more than you need, cranberries freeze beautifully. Set some aside for baking after the holidays. A cranberry-orange loaf will be just as appreciated when the oven has considerably fewer obligations.
