An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6507. I Tried Keurig’s First-Ever Espresso Machine—Is It Worth Adding To Your Coffee Routine?

I’ve owned a Keurig, I’ve owned a Nespresso, and I’ve spent way too much money on coffee shop runs in between. Needless to say, I’m an expert on the subject. So when I heard that Keurig was launching its first-ever espresso machine, my interest was piqued. Could the brand that turned single-serve coffee into the household standard successfully switch up its game?

Keurig’s latest and possibly greatest innovation—a two-in-one single-serve coffee maker and espresso machine called the Alta System—will turn your home kitchen into a coffee shop thanks to a multifunctional design that brews everything from regular coffee to espresso, cappuccinos, and lattes. It comes with a built-in milk frother and functions exclusively on the new plastic- and aluminum-free pods (sustainability, hallelujah!).

Here’s whether the Keurig Alta System lives up to the hype, how it compares to other machines, and whether it deserves a spot on your own kitchen coffee bar.

Let’s go a little more in-depth, shall we? The Keurig Alta System is the brand’s new single-serve coffee and espresso machine that does a lot more than your standard K-Cup brewer. Unlike the brand’s traditional lineup, which uses K-Cup pods, the Alta introduces an entirely new innovation: AltaRounds. Your machine can read a code on the AltaRounds and adjust its brew settings accordingly, whether that’s pressure, temperature, or the water-to-coffee ratio. (K-Cups are still compatible with the Alta).

The integrated milk frother is another major upgrade for Keurig, letting you make hot and cold foam.

The Keurig Alta System is $499.99, which, yes, is pricier than other Keurig models. However, classic espresso machines can run you upwards of $1,000.

As for the AltaRounds, they’re sold in boxes of eight, ranging from $9.99 to $10.99 depending on the variety. If you wanna break that up by coffee, it’s about $1.25 to $1.37 a cup. Not too shabby.

As someone who is impatient and terrible at reading directions (hello, your type B friend reporting for duty), I wasn’t overly optimistic I’d figure it out that quickly. But it’s actually an easy device to navigate, thanks to the convenient LED screen that walks you through the whole process.

I was immediately transfixed by the machine. I texted my boyfriend, “I’m in love with it,” before it even finished brewing my first coffee. The Alta feels so much chicer on my countertops, and the pods are smaller and store more easily. Once I finally took that first sip, I was ready to toss my old Keurig in the trash (respectfully).

The drip coffee and espresso shots taste like something straight from an award-winning barista. I love the flexibility to make a black coffee one day and an iced caramel latte the next. And the milk frother just takes the entire thing to the next level.

Listen, $500 for a coffee machine is a lot. And maybe because of that, this isn’t an upgrade you can make immediately. Still, the Keurig Alta System is worth the hype; if you can swap your classic single-serve maker for it, you should. It checks literally every box—it’s more aesthetic, more versatile, and more sustainable.

The only caveat is if you’re the type of person who exclusively drinks drip coffee. In that case, it might not be worth the splurge. But if you want to cosplay as a barista and whip up new creations, from frothy cappuccinos to iced lattes and espresso martinis, the Alta provides all the room to experiment (and it will ultimately save you money on those $10 coffee runs).

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: As of 11:15 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA and the Aerospace Corporation both predict that the Swift observatory could have reentered Earth's atmosphere by now. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall.NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft could have already met its demise as of Wednesday morning, though no official confirmation has been shared.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6501. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!

#6499. How Flavored Syrup Became a Coffee-Shop Culture War

For some coffee shop customers, premade syrups are now a major red flag. It presents a new opportunity for small business owners.

In a TikTok video with over 82,000 likes, the person behind the camera zooms into the shelves at a Pennsylvania coffee shop, three rows stacked with an array of Torani syrups in flavors like blueberry, brown-sugar cinnamon, English toffee, and salted caramel. “I just know my latte isn’t going to be good,” the caption reads. Across social media, similar sentiments appear. “If I see these at a cafe, I’m walking out immediately,” says one tweet, co-signed by many commenters. In a multipart video series, another creator documents her journey of replacing all of her Torani syrups with ones from small businesses instead. Last year, the niche food newsletter Unsnackable published what was described as a “Torani tirade.”

It’s not just a Torani problem, though the brand — by virtue of its market dominance — tends to get the most flack on social media. While some people seem to prefer competitor Monin, it, too, draws backlash over allegations of tasting “like chemicals.” The problem, for some drinkers of dessert-like specialty beverages, is premade syrups across the board.

For a certain sect of consumers, they’ve become a coffee shop red flag, a sign that a so-called “specialty” establishment asking them to fork over $8 plus tip for a latte is unfairly cutting corners when it comes to quality or craft. For these consumers, mass-market syrups now symbolize exactly that: They’re synonymous with coffee chains and corporations, the kind of impersonal institutions that many people are trying to get away from when they patronize a small business. The flip side: For independently owned coffee shops across the country, house-made syrup now represents a major opportunity.

When Carrie and Dennis Medina first envisioned their coffee shop, Room Service, in Ventura, California, they thought they would take an approach similar to the one at Sightglass Coffee, where they’d both gotten their start. “Very purist, with no syrups, no specialty drinks,” Dennis says. They imagined eight kinds of pour-over coffee and an emphasis on single-origin beans, since the couple also runs a roastery. “We said we’re never gonna do cream tops; we’re never gonna do these crazy drinks,” Carrie says. But in the first week alone, every customer was asking for them.

Now, Room Service offers 10 to 12 different syrups at any given time (and six different cream tops), all of them made in-house. It offers drinks such as a cinnamon roll latte topped with a cinnamon roll, and a honey cornbread latte with an ube cream top. “I hear that question all the time,” Dennis says. “‘Hey, do you guys make your syrups in-house?’” To him, a shop that isn’t trying to do at least the basics — like vanilla — in-house is “falling behind what the times are pushing for.”

The demand for syrups and other embellishments is so intense that the Medinas have brought on a full-time prep person who works exclusively on “all these things that we do in-house that make us special,” Carrie says. Room Service’s PSL, for example, starts with kabocha squash. It’s roasted, blended with spices such as cloves and cinnamon, and cooked into syrup, a process that takes two days. Echoing a sentiment that seems common among coffee shop owners right now, Carrie describes their current approach as “not necessarily the coffee shop we wanted, but it’s more like the coffee shop we have to be.” And if the market demands syrups and cream tops, then the Medinas wanted to ensure that the intention and emphasis on quality that they applied to their coffee beans also carried over.

In 2025, Michael Smith opened Trust Coffee Co. in Bay Village, Ohio, taking over, remodeling, and rebranding an older coffee shop. He, like the Medinas, imagined a more “pour-over, third-wave” style establishment. “But I’ve been a business owner for a long time,” says Smith, who also runs a restaurant and a catering business. “I’ve realized over the years that your customers tell you more about who you are than who you actually think you are.” His customers, it turned out, wanted seasonal syrups in niche flavors like maple rosemary, caramelized banana, and strawberry rhubarb.

The purist is no longer coffee’s north star; the maximalist is.

Syrups like Monin, which the shop’s previous iteration used, “serve a purpose in the industry,” Smith says, but he wanted more control over the menu. The two full-time pastry chefs from Smith’s other businesses oversee the shop’s syrups. “It’s become such a huge thing,” he says: Every time Trust’s social media manager posts a new syrup, the line is out the door for a week. “It sets us apart,” he explains.

When Sabrina Kaylor opened the first location of Bizarre Coffee in Canton, Georgia in 2020, the shop used bottled syrups. She hadn’t worked in coffee prior, and she said that approach felt like the norm at the time. “It allowed us to hone our craft and learn what we were doing,” she says. Over time, Kaylor — who’s quite active on the company’s official social media platforms — noticed that the tenor of the conversation was changing: In the immediate post-COVID years, people were making more things at home and there was more pride to be gained in “scratch-made.” With her business becoming known for lattes in flavors such as blueberry, banana, and guava, Kaylor decided to shift toward more house-made syrups. Previously, her customers didn’t ask about their sourcing, but now, they ask all the time.

As much as there is a sense of valor in the entirely from-scratch approach, Kaylor retains some skepticism about the current torrent of Torani and Monin backlash. Today, 90 percent of Bizarre’s drinks use house-made syrups, though one of its best-selling drinks still relies on the bottled stuff; Bizarre’s menu is extensive and making everything in-house would be a significant investment of labor. On the part of coffee shops, “I think a lot of [the house-made syrup conversation] is marketing, quite honestly,” Kaylor says. As for the bandwagoning that is all the anti-Torani memes, “I think it’s part of consumer behavior,” she says. And that, she acknowledges, can be really “discouraging” for small business owners.

In a sense, that’s what the premade-versus-house-made-syrup conversation boils down to: the stand between small businesses and big ones. For more consumers, the economic and social conditions of the current moment have inspired increased skepticism toward the influence of corporations and private equity in the food and beverage world.

The Minnesota coffee shop Little Joy has become famous across social media for posting the recipes of its signature drinks in detailed DIY videos. It has since launched a membership program through which other coffee shop owners can purchase its recipes, scaled up for commercial usage; gain access to training videos; and sell its drinks without even needing to attribute them to Little Joy, though the ones that would like to can pin their use of Little Joy’s recipes to a Drink Finder map.

Yes, these might just be recipes for syrups and foams, but in an interview with Eater’s industry newsletter Pre Shift earlier this year, Little Joy owner Cody Larson described the system as a way to build solidarity among independent businesses. “The big coffee chains, they’re never gonna do house-made syrups, so I think that’s where independent shops can get a leg up,” he said. “Ultimately, the chains are our competition... If independent shops can, in any way possible, raise the bar across the board, that’s good for all independent shops, including us.”

It’s hard to look at the drinks coming out of specialty coffee shops today — fluffy with foam, flavored to emulate nuanced desserts like princess cake and tiramisu— and not think of the Starbucks Frappuccino. The combination of app-ordering and social media “hack” culture have mainstreamed super-elaborate beverage requests, allowing Starbucks and coffee chains like it to become purveyors of highly complicated customizable beverages, mainstreaming the mindset of the aforementioned “hyperflavor.”

When it comes to why consumers have moved away from the single-origin pour-over approach at shops like his, “my guess is that these are a lot of people who used to be Starbucks loyalists and they’re looking for something that’s more local,” Smith says. “It’s a trend across everything where people want local, and we’re able to provide what Starbucks did, but in a more high-quality, more local way.”

Intentionality is what people are gravitating towards, especially as prices rise. If consumers are spending so much on a drink that’s undeniably a luxury, then they want to know that every part of that drink has been made carefully. And if they’re going to make the trip to a new, independent shop, they want to know that the offerings there aren’t the ones they can get anywhere, made with easily attainable, big-brand flavorings. For small coffee shops, the key to success could be as simple as syrup.

#6498. Hot Honey Brussels Sprouts

These honey-glazed brussels sprouts are saucy, tangy-sweet, and have a bit of kick. Caramelizing the honey gives it a deeper, toastier sweetness. Vinegar, red pepper flakes, and a good dose of butter transform it into a sticky sauce that seeps into the nooks of each and every sprout. The recipe makes a generous amount: Use it all, or save some for drizzling on pizza a few days later.

The trick to perfectly charred brussels sprouts? Preheat the sheet pan, then arrange the halved sprouts cut side down on the hot metal. It might feel a little fussy flipping each sprout onto its flat side, but the deeply browned results are worth it.

Make the glaze while the sprouts roast or up to five days ahead, then toss everything together just before serving to preserve those crispy edges.

Glossy and pourable, about the consistency of warm maple syrup—not thick like caramel. The honey will foam as it cooks, and the mixture will bubble aggressively when you add the vinegar. Both are normal. The glaze will thicken a bit as it cools, so don’t worry if it seems slightly thin while still bubbling.

They have a noticeable kick, but they’re more tangy-sweet than fiery. The honey and butter temper the chile flakes. If you’re sensitive to spice, use less than the suggested ¾ tsp. or leave the flakes out entirely.

Place a rimmed baking sheet on bottom rack of oven; preheat to 450°. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, and ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large bowl; sprinkle with ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and season with freshly ground black pepper.

Carefully remove baking sheet from oven. Using tongs, arrange brussels sprouts cut-side down on hot baking sheet. Roast brussels on bottom rack until softened and deeply browned, 15–25 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring ¼ cup honey to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring often, until honey is a deep amber color but not burnt (it will be foamy, that’s okay), 3–4 minutes.

Remove from heat and add ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar (it will bubble up quite aggressively) and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes; whisk until sauce is smooth. Return saucepan to medium heat and add 3 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, whisking constantly, until glaze is glossy, bubbling, and slightly thickened, 3–4 minutes.

Transfer roasted brussels sprouts to a large bowl. Add half the hot honey glaze and scallions and toss to combine. Taste and add more glaze if desired. Transfer to a platter and top with lemon zest. Serve remaining glaze alongside.

Do ahead: Glaze can be made 5 days ahead; refrigerate after cooling.

#6497. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6495. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

#6493. Sausage Stuffing Recipe

This sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath.

Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch.

Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

This stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape.

Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time?

You can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

#6492. Chatpata Potato Chip Tower

Cookbook author Rachel Gurjar doesn’t usually jump on food trends, but the potato chip tower called to her. “Chips are already great as is, but I knew a version inspired by chana chor—a fiery street snack made from flattened, fried black chickpeas tossed with onions, chiles, lemon, and chaat masala—would kick it up a notch,” she writes in her debut title, East to East. Chatpata is a Hindi word that means salty, sour, spicy, and sweet at the same time, and this chatpata potato chip tower absolutely lives up to its name. While you can use any potato chips you like—or even substitute tortilla chips, pita chips, or fried pita bread—Gurjar recommends thick kettle-cooked chips, as they stay crispy longer.

#6491. Mexican Seafood and Natural Wines Are in the Spotlight at This New NYC Restaurant

A stacked tuna tostada, puckering shrimp aguachile, and more seafood dishes stun at El Camarón Peludo

Known for their roasted and slow-cooked meats at Taqueria Ramirez, Tania Apolinar and Giovanni Cervantes partnered with chef Carlos Barrera to open a new seafood-focused wine bar this year. Here’s what a full day of prep looks like at El Camarón Peludo in the West Village.

First, fresh shrimp from Sinaloa, Mexico; Ecuador; and more locales are de-shelled and de-veined for three central shrimp dishes. Then, Cervantes starts the fresh salsa for the day, taste testing and comparing each batch to the salsa from last week to make sure the flavor is consistent. A bright red salsa is mixed with mayo to create the sauce on the camarones zarandeados, a shrimp version of a fish dish from the Pacific coast of Mexico that is usually grilled in a flat wire grill basket.

Upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

Back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

Watch the team at the Mexican seafood wine bar prepare tostadas, tacos, and flavor-packed aguachile in the newest episode of Now Open.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6489. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

Adapted from East to East: Recipes and Stories From Mumbai to New York by Rachel Gurjar. Copyright © 2026. Available from Chronicle Books.

Featured in “Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City.”

#6488. Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Shows Water Ice Behaves the Same Across Alien Star Systems

Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWSTâs findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.

Typically, water ice is pretty easy to spot for astronomers. In infrared, which is JWSTâs specialty, it absorbs light very clearly at 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 microns in wavelength. Weâve known that for years, and have seen evidence of it in regular comets based strictly on our solar system, such as Hartley 2.

But when JWST looked at 3I/ATLAS, it clearly showed the 3.0 micron absorption line, but the 1.5 and 2.0 ones were surprisingly weak or absent. It also featured a blue near-infrared continuum slope across 1.15â2.50 microns that wasnât typical of the other comets zooming around our solar system. These discrepancies led some observers to question whether 3I/ATLAS actually contained any water ice at all, but the new paper with higher resolution observations quickly put paid to that idea.

Fraser talks about the orbital mechanics of 3I/ATLAS

To prove that it does, indeed, contain water ice, the research team modeled how light scatters through âmixedâ particles that contain both water and dust. This lined up much more closely with the observed spectral lines of 3I/ATLAS, proving that, instead of pure water ice with a clear pattern, the ice is locked up into microscopic grains that blend water and dark rocky minerals, such as pyroxene and carbon.

Light can only travel so far through these aggregates before hitting some dust, causing a shortened optical pathway. That, in turn, mutes the absorption features at the 1.5 and 2.0 micron level, while the longer 3.0 micron wavelength is still able to pass straight through. The tiny grains also scatter shorter wavelengths more effectively, which explains the general blue hue that JWST saw.

In fact, JWST observed this interstellar visitor at three different times during its journey through our solar system, starting when it was about 3.31 astronomical units (AU) out from perihelion all the way through when it was about 5.65 AU past perihelion. And the differences in 3I/ATLASâs spectra were noticeable at each stage. After perihelion, the grains of ice and dust appeared to include a second population of larger, micron-sized, ice-rich aggregates.

Fraser talks about what would happen if we could catch an interstellar object.

Also, after perihelion the researchers noticed a new optical effect known as a Fresnel reflection near 3.1 microns, which indicated that there was also âcrystallineâ water ice in 3I/ATLAS. This differs from the normal, disorganized type of ice normally seen, as its water molecules arrange themselves in neat crystalline lattices rather than in a jumble. According to the paper, these layers were only visible after perihelion either because the Sun itself warmed the surface layers causing them to reconfigure into a crystal, or the solar energy caused the outer dust to blast away, revealing cleaner underlying crystalline structures that were previously hidden.

But perhaps the most interesting part of the paper was the parallels it was able to draw with our own solar system. The infrared patterns of 3I/ATLAS match certain types of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) in our own solar system. These balls of ice and rock are the planetary leftovers that float out beyond Neptune in the Kuiper belt, and JWST has already spent plenty of time staring at them. Previously, researchers had seen the same 3.0 micron absorption pattern without the 1.5 and 2.0 micron features, but had thought those patterns might be attributable to complex hydrocarbons or organics. Turns out it might just have been dusty ice all along, at least according to the new paper.

Itâs unclear whether there will ever be another opportunity like this in JWSTâs operational lifetime. But thereâs still plenty left to understand about our most recent interstellar visitor. As more and more scientists continue to analyze the data that was collected during 3I/ATLASâs sojourn through our system, thereâs undoubtedly more to be discovered about our latest interstellar visitor, and especially how it can explain more about our own solar system.

SwRI - SwRI-led study uses Webb to compare interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS with icy bodies in our solar system

S. Protopapa - JWST Reveals Refractory-rich Water Ice in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS: Evidence for a Continuum of Grain Properties across Protoplanetary Disks

UT - 3I/ATLAS Has An Extreme Taste For Heavy Water

UT - 3I/ATLAS Is Very Actively Releasing Water

#6487. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

#6486. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

Hungry for even more stories to sink your teeth into?

The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#6485. A Mighty Wind Blew Away Gas and Made Early Galaxies Brighter

Only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, during the Cosmic Dawn, bright galaxies populated the Universe in numbers higher than expected. The JWST showed that these galaxies formed very dense, compact clusters of stars. Why their star formation was concentrated in such dense clusters is a puzzle, as is the brightness of their host galaxies.

A pair of researchers may have figured it out. Their work is titled "LyÎ± Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The authors are Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith. Lead author Menon is a research fellow at the Flatiron Instituteâs Center for Computational Astrophysics, and co-author Smith is an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas.

The Lyman-Alpha (LyÎ±) radiation in the paper's title is a very important factor in astrophysics. It's produced when an electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from excited to ground state. Since hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the Universe, LyÎ± is a fundamental way to probe the Universe's earliest galaxies, including the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM).

"Observations with the JWST in lensed fields have revealed that galaxies at cosmic dawn may concentrate their star formation in highly dense, compact, star clusters," the authors write. "The high columns and low metallicities encountered in their birth environments suggest that LyÎ± radiation pressure may be crucial to their formation and evolution."

These panels show some of the bright and dense star clusters the JWST found in the early Universe, only about 460 million years after the Big. The panel on the right shows their location in SPT0615-JD1, a strongly-lensed galaxy. Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, L. Bradley (STScI), A. Adamo (Stockholm University) and the Cosmic Spring collaboration

âOur results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,â lead author Menon said. âIt can sort of clear the âfog,â allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.â

LyÎ±'s utility as a diagnostic tool also explains its powerful ability to push dust and gas away so quickly. LyÎ± radiation is different than others. Typically, when an atom absorbs energy, it re-emits it at a different wavelength. But hydrogen atoms absorb LyÎ± and then re-emit it again almost instantaneously, where it interacts with more hydrogen. This absorption-emission cycle makes it a powerful diagnostic tool, and it also gives LyÎ± the ability to bully hydrogen gas.

Astrophysicists knew this, but understanding its effect on a large scale was difficult.

âWeâve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,â Menon says. âBut weâve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.â

Researchers have tried to incorporate it into models, but Lyman-alpha resists those attempts. Some haven't even tried to include it. "The oversight is related to its high dimensionality and complexity, as well as the inherently demanding computational requirements for modeling it self-consistently," the authors write.

The reason it's difficult to model is precisely because of its repeating cycle of absorption and emission. But difficult isn't synonymous with impossible.

Menon and Smith didn't try to simulate it. Instead, they took snapshots from existing simulations and got busy calculating the force necessary to explain the snapshots. "In this study, we address this question by postprocessing snapshots from radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of dense star-cluster-forming clouds with a range of dust abundances using the COLT Monte Carlo code," they explain. COLT stands for Cosmic Lyman-alpha Transfer. Study co-author Aaron Smith is COLT's original creator, and he wrote it to "simulate the production and escape of LyÎ± from hydrodynamical simulations," according to the COLT website.

In short, they examined simulation snapshots of star-forming regions in the early Universe, and calculated the amount of LyÎ± necessary to explain what they saw.

These are multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas).

The results showed that Lyman-alpha radiation wasn't strong enough to blow away the gas in the dense star-forming regions found by the JWST. The gravity from the dense gas in those filaments was too strong for Lyman-alpha to overcome. But beyond those dense filaments, it was powerful enough to blow away the more diffuse gas and the dust.

This graphic shows how Lyman-Alpha was able to blow away gas and dust that obscured early galaxies and their dense star clusters. Image Credit: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation

The authors outline two simple conclusions in their paper: "LyÎ± radiation pressure is unlikely to preclude efficient star formation," and "LyÎ± radiation pressure can drive dynamically significant winds once star formation saturates."

"Therefore, our results suggest that the SFE is likely to remain high in the dense star clusters forming at high-z. On the other hand, a significant fraction of the volume-filling gas can be ejected by LyÎ± radiation pressure, suggesting implications for the visibility of light from the cluster, ionizing photon escape, and launching outflows from the galaxy," the researchers write in their paper.

So once star formation had proceeded far enough in these dense clusters, Lyman-alpha made them visible by blowing away the rest of the gas.

âWhen the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,â Menon says. "That cleared away the gas obscuring the dense clusters, making them visible."
