#6398. A Hidden Cancer-Killing Mechanism Could Change the Future of Immunotherapy

An immune protein called perforin can turn iron against cancer cells in laboratory experiments, suggesting a possible route to more effective immunotherapy.

The immune system can attack cancer cells by punching holes in their outer membranes and sending in enzymes that kill them. Research led by the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center shows that the protein making those openings can also kill tumor cells on its own.

That protein, perforin, is made by T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. For decades, scientists have known that it allows protein-cutting enzymes called granzymes to enter target cells and trigger their death. But the new study, published in Cell, found that tumor cells could be killed even when major granzymes were missing. Losing perforin, however, caused a catastrophic failure of the immune response against tumors in the study.

“If T cells and NK cells are the soldiers of the immune system, perforin is the weapon, and granzymes are the ammunition,” said co-senior study author Weiping Zou, MD, PhD, Charles B. de Nancrede Professor of Pathology, Immunology, Biology, and Surgery at the University of Michigan (U-M). “At least, that’s what the classic understanding was.”

To investigate perforin’s role, the researchers combined three approaches: genetic and biochemical experiments in cells grown in the laboratory, studies in mice, and data from people with cancer.

“We wanted to know if perforin, by itself, can do the job,” Zou said. “The answer is yes.”

The laboratory experiments traced that killing to ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Beyond making holes in a cancer cell’s membrane, perforin interfered with its iron uptake, causing iron to accumulate inside the cell, including in its mitochondria, structures that help supply energy. The excess iron rapidly oxidized lipids, the fatty molecules that help make up membranes.

Ferroptosis occurs when lipid peroxides, or oxidized fats, build up in the membranes surrounding cells and their internal structures. It differs from apoptosis, the form of cell death triggered by granzymes, and from pyroptosis, which is often caused by bacterial infection.

“Our findings show, for the first time, that perforin can independently induce ferroptosis in tumor cells,” said co-senior author Ilona Kryczek, PhD, a researcher at U-M. “This work changes our understanding of one of the longest-held mechanisms of T cell and NK cell-mediated tumor clearance.”

Zou and Kryczek worked closely with co-senior author Judy Lieberman, PhD, of Harvard Medical School, one of the international pioneers of cytotoxic lymphocyte research, the study of immune cells that kill other cells.

In the mouse studies, animals fed an iron-rich diet had slower tumor progression, a result related to their perforin expression. That observation comes with an important caution for anyone considering what it might mean for cancer treatment.

“We need to be very cautious here,” Zou said. “That’s because some cancer types enjoy an iron-rich diet. For those tumors, and we don’t totally know which ones yet, an iron-rich diet may accelerate progression.”

The human data offered another connection between perforin and cancer outcomes. Patients with higher perforin expression had better survival and better responses to immune checkpoint blockade, treatments that release molecular brakes on immune cells. These findings were associations in patient data.

“It is a new way of thinking about how immune cells kill tumors,” said Hannah Bell, PhD, the study’s first author, until recently a postdoctoral researcher in Zou’s lab and now an assistant professor in Molecular and Integrative Physiology at U-M.

Ferroptosis was formally introduced over a decade ago, so scientists still know less about it than more established forms of cell death.

“It’s a very hot area that needs a lot of research,” Zou said.

In 2019, his group was the first to report the immune system’s role in ferroptosis in tumors, highlighting the pathway as a potential target for immune checkpoint therapy. Previous work has also shown that immune checkpoint blockade can enhance T cell-mediated ferroptosis, making that connection a likely direction for further research.

It is still too soon to say how the new findings might translate into clinical applications.

“If we can understand what makes a tumor cell susceptible to perforin, we may be able to increase the effectiveness of immunotherapy,” Zou said.

The team plans to examine the cell death mechanism more closely, test whether multiple routes to cell death could be working together, and explore potential clinical applications.

“At the end of the day, the whole goal of different forms of cancer therapies — immunotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy — is to kill tumor cells,” Zou said. “Improving our understanding of cell death, like we do in this study, is so fundamental and so important. That’s why we’re going to continue to push on this.”

Reference: “Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity” by Hannah N. Bell, Kavya Nair, Kole Tison, Peng Liao, Hongwei Lei, Marwa O. El-Derany, Ayijiang Yisimayi, Haiwei Zhang, Ryan Rebernick, Weichao Wang, Yoshitaka Adachi, Cristina Castillo, Nupur K. Das, Jinsu An, Vivien R. Sutton, Xun Lin, Heng Lin, Xinghao Wang, Yunfei Li, Linda Vatan, Amr Aboud, Shuang Wei, Miguel Gijon, Samantha Goodwin, Yatrik M. Shah, Ilona Kryczek, Joseph A. Trapani, Margarida Barroso, Judy Lieberman and Weiping Zou, 23 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.062

Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6396. Scientists Zapped Mouse Brains With Lasers to Give Them Phantom Visions

This illusion of reality could be playing a game-changing role in the evolution of perception—ours included.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

How do you make a mouse hallucinate? (And why would you even try?)

Hyeyoung Shin, PhD, an assistant professor of neuroscience at Seoul National University, turned to mice to help explain what makes one person perceive reality differently from another. Take the great dress debate from 2015, for example, when people across social media argued over whether an online post depicted a white-and-gold or a blue-and-black garment (Spoiler: It was the latter).

Shin herself wondered what her brain was doing when she looked at the dress image online. More than 10 years later, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, she was finally able to explain why.

In their study, Shin and her colleagues zapped the brains of six mice with ultraprecise holographic lasers, targeting a tiny cluster of cells in the brain’s first layer of image-sensing neurons, an area called V1. Researchers asked whether sparking those cells alone could make the brain “see” something that wasn’t really there.

The animals’ brains lit up as if they were seeing phantom shapes, like the Kanizsa triangle, where Pac-Man cutouts trick you into seeing a triangle that isn’t actually present. The team baptized these cells “IC-encoder neurons,” because a spark from them can ripple outward, recruiting tens of thousands of other neurons to finish the picture.

Shin says she hadn’t expected this “filling-in” to happen so early, right in the brain’s first visual processing area.

That means reality is in the eye of the beholder. It implies that “perception is not a direct recording of reality, but a process of inference,” says Shin. In neuroscience, inference means the brain makes its best guess about what’s out there—filling in perception gaps and leaning on past experience. She’s quick to dismiss going so far as to call reality a “controlled hallucination,” though, since hallucination means experiencing things that don’t exist in any form. “Instead, illusion—and perception in general—is the brain interpreting sensory evidence based on your beliefs about the sensory world,” she says.

It turns out our brains create an illusion of reality based on both our previous experiences and the evolutionary design of our primary visual cortex. Located at the back of the brain, where it receives signals from our eyes, this first layer of image sensing (called V1) doesn’t just take pictures. In fact, it helps decide—if not dictate—what we see.

And that’s crucial, because this design enables our ability to make decisions quickly based on how we perceive the world around us, scientists say. Otherwise, we might spend too much time trying to recognize important stimuli in our environment, such as danger.

In everyday life, we mostly do agree on what we see. Even in the dress debate—a perception anomaly in itself—no one saw red or fuchsia. The fight was only between two specific color combinations. So are our brains all running on the same basic code?

This story has reporting from Stav Dimitropoulos.

#6394. “This Should Not Happen”: Scientists Discover a Strange New Way To Control Atoms

Scientists have used radio waves to control the magnetic spin of a single atomic nucleus, achieving a result that challenges their understanding of how atomic magnetism works. The experiment, conducted at Delft University of Technology and published in Nature Communications, demonstrates that nuclear spin can be manipulated under conditions where researchers did not expect it to respond.

Unlike the relatively strong magnetism associated with electrons, nuclear magnetism is extremely weak and more isolated from its surroundings. “By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons,” says lead researcher Sander Otte. “But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.”

To investigate magnetism at the atomic scale, Otte’s team uses a modified scanning tunneling microscope capable of directing electrical signals at individual atoms. Previous experiments primarily examined electron spin, which is easier to detect and manipulate. Nuclear spin could be observed indirectly through the hyperfine interaction, a quantum coupling between the magnetic properties of an electron and the nucleus.

In the latest experiment, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues applied two signals simultaneously, one targeting the electron and another targeting the nucleus. By examining their effects separately, the researchers discovered that they could flip the nuclear spin even when it was largely disentangled from the electron spin. This contradicted their expectation that the nucleus would not respond independently to the microscope’s electrical signals.

“According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen,” says Otte. “The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.”

The researchers achieved this control by adapting double magnetic resonance, an established technique, to work with a single atom. The method allowed them to address the nucleus and electron independently using signals tuned to their respective magnetic resonances. In quantum mechanics, spin can change between specific allowed states, and each transition requires a signal with the appropriate frequency.

“You can compare it to the strings of a guitar,” Vennema explains. “Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The ‘notes’ of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.”

Nuclear spins are promising candidates for storing quantum information because they are relatively well protected from external disturbances that can disrupt delicate quantum states. The ability to control an individual nuclear spin could eventually support new methods for storing and reading quantum information, although practical applications remain a future possibility.

For now, the experiment leaves a fundamental question unanswered: What physical mechanism allows the nuclear spin to respond when its coupling to the electron spin is insufficient to explain the observed behavior? Understanding that process will require further investigation.

“Back to the drawing board, then,” says Otte. “That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out.”

Reference: “Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe” by Hester G. Vennema, Cristina Mier, Evert W. Stolte, Leonard Edens, Jinwon Lee and Sander Otte, 24 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78801-5

#6393. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

P.K. Masonick et al. The repeated evolution of anti-bat bioacoustics in hawkmoths. Proceedings of the Royal Society B. 2026. doi: 10.1098/rspb.2026.2303

#6392. The 6 Best Laptops You Can Buy

From wallet-friendly buys to big-money AI and content-creation powerhouses, we ranked today’s best portable computers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether you're in the mood for a movie night, want to keep your social media game strong, plan an online grocery run, or settle in for a marathon gaming session, a good laptop is a trusty sidekick. Choosing one, however, is not a quick or simple decision. You’ll need to find the right machine to supercharge your productivity or fuel your passion for gaming. Just beware: Picking the wrong machine could get in the way of your passions instead of enhancing them.

Luckily, the laptop market offers options for every need and budget, and we've handpicked the best for you. Still, before you whip out that credit card, you first need to choose sides in the age-old Mac versus Windows debate. Apple's MacBooks shine with top-tier build quality and a rock-solid platform. They're a dream come true for those who don't rely on Windows-specific software.

However, some folks think that Apple's ecosystem feels a bit like the Hotel California—you can check out anytime you like, but you can never leave. Separately, despite Apple's best efforts, the Mac ecosystem still has some software limitations, especially for avid PC gamers.

Now, let's talk style. Do you want a traditional laptop or one that can transform into a superhero? If you desire a laptop that moonlights as a tablet, a 2-in-1 device is your new BFF. These nifty gadgets come with a keyboard that vanishes when you don't need it, making them perfect for streaming, unleashing your inner artist on the touchscreen, and more. But here's the catch: touchscreens can sometimes make you miss the crystal-clear clarity of a traditional screen, especially when you're knee-deep in an epic writing session.

We pored over the specs and reviews of dozens of the latest laptops to assemble this list of the best notebooks you can buy today. We looked for laptops we would be happy to use ourselves, while also finding models that fit a range of budgets and preferences. Our tech writers personally own and use several of these machines at home, including the MacBook Pro, the Microsoft Surface lineup, and MacBook Neo, and can vouch for long-term quality and durability.

The base model of Apple’s 2026 MacBook Pro line is a basic refresh built around the brand’s newest processor, the M6. Even without any flashy new features, the upgrade further enhances what was already the best laptop for anyone who needs a laptop with serious power. With an unbeatable mix of timelessly elegant design, top-tier craftsmanship, outstanding performance, and long battery life, this is the complete package.

On the performance front, the entry-level MacBook Pro handled everything we threw at it—from toggling between multiple apps to running blockbuster games like Cyberpunk 2077 on high settings. And, unlike its Windows-based rivals with similar hardware capabilities, the MacBook Pro can easily deliver a full day of mixed use on a single charge. Its 2-nanometer chip architecture brings a welcome power bump without sacrificing energy efficiency.

The M6 MacBook Pro is only available with a 14.2-inch display. Much more powerful variants with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are available in two screen sizes—14.2- and 16.2-inch. With more CPU and GPU cores and significantly higher memory bandwidth, the M5 Pro and Max can handle heavier workflows—from AI-related tasks to high-resolution video editing projects—anytime, anywhere.

It’s worth saying that, while we recommend the MacBook Pro for everyone, it may be overkill for folks who only use their laptop for the basics—email, Google Docs, web browsing, and streaming video. The word “Pro” is in the name for a reason: The more powerful specs give you the compute you need for creative projects like image or video editing, audio production, or local AI workflows. If those things aren’t a part of your day-to-day, you may be better off with moving down the MacBook line to the M5 MacBook Air or even my budget pick, the MacBook Neo.

Apple genuinely shook up the entire computing world when it launched the MacBook Neo, a budget-tier Mac built around an iPhone processor that starts at less than $700. Up to this point, the cheapest new Mac was traditionally the MacBook Air, which cost just over $1,000, which forced Mac users to spend a pretty penny to gain access to their preferred operating system, even if they didn’t need the power it offered.

You’d think that a “budget” Mac would somehow feel less than to justify the higher spend for an Air, but the truth is that the Neo is realistically more than enough machine for folks who just need the basics. Compared to similarly priced Windows machines, the Neo offers stellar all-around performance and great battery life, making it kind of a no-brainer for a lot of folks. It’s a bit thicker than an Air, but makes up for it on the style front with a small array of iMac-esque colorways.

Make no mistake, this is not a powerhouse, though: the Neo runs on the A18 Pro chip, which is not the newest mobile processor, and only features 8GB of RAM in the base configuration, which is enough for browsing and email, but will likely slow down and struggle with anything complex. While it drives the price up a bit, I would urge most folks to go with the slightly pricier 512GB version, which also adds a TouchID fingerprint sensor. Even with the base model, though, the Neo is cooler, and a better buy than just about any other machine under $1,000 you’ll find on this side of a Black Friday sale.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop is a formidable PC alternative to our top Apple pick, pairing beautiful design and craftsmanship with top-tier Qualcomm silicon that delivers stellar performance at a similar price. Weighing either just under or slightly over three pounds, depending on the screen size, this metal-clad notebook is impressively light and slim, given its hardware specs and performance.

Hardware-wise, the Microsoft Surface Laptop impresses with a sharp PixelSense touchscreen, the latest Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus or X2 Elite chip, plenty of memory, and a comprehensive set of futureproof wired and wireless connectivity features. In my experience, both the entry-level and top-spec versions delivered excellent all-around performance and long battery life.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop comes in three screen sizes—13-, 13.8-, and 15-inch—unlike the MacBook Air or Pro and any PC laptop rival. The 13-inch version with a six-core Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 chip is the most affordable. Upping your budget for a 13.8- or 15-inch model, alongside a more powerful chip, will get you a sharper and brighter display panel with a higher refresh rate and Dolby Vision HDR support.

The recently launched Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with the brand-new Nvidia RTX Spark chip is the PC laptop to get if you are a PC power user with a big upgrade budget. The notebook’s first-of-its-kind silicon makes it great for demanding workflows—from AI-related tasks to AAA gameplay.

The Asus ROG Strix G16 is an upgrade-worthy gaming laptop for players looking to balance serious gaming specs with portability. With gaming laptops, there’s often a fine line between making an underpowered machine that lacks the specs to keep up with even a budget-tier desktop, and a huge “desktop replacement” that’s too heavy to carry on a daily basis. The Strix G16 walks that line well, delivering strong performance while keeping things relatively light.

Gaming laptops generally run heavier than performance machines, so while six pounds may sound like a lot, it's not that bad when you factor in the power at your disposal. The configuration we tested, with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU, an Intel Core Ultra 9 processor, and 32 GB of RAM, will handle new games on high or ultra settings with ease. They'll also look great on a 2.5K G-Sync display that maxes out at 240Hz, ensuring smooth, lifelike gameplay.

Depending on your budget, you can scale this laptop's hardware up or down to meet your needs. If you can live with slightly less performance, there's a more budget-friendly sub-$1,500 version with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU. On the other end, this monstrously powerful config costs nearly $4,000, but your games will look absolutely incredible.

Chromebooks are historically known for being a cheap, basic notebook option, which has been widely adopted for young students who need a school-only machine. But with tech prices going the way they’ve been going and Google releasing a new, more powerful class of AI-focused Googlebooks starting at $899, that price advantage has largely evaporated. Given that, we’re only inclined to recommend high-performance Chromebooks, rather than the cheapest models.

For $750, Lenovo’s Chromebook Plus 14 is a high-end Chromebook, but still feels fairly budget-friendly compared to the wider world of laptops. It features a MediaTek chip and 16 GB of RAM, which gives you pretty snappy responsiveness for basic email and web browsing, and across ChromeOS-friendly Android apps.

The best part, I think, is its display: A sharp, 14-inch OLED touchscreen that makes streams look great. For work and school, it also has a surprisingly good high-resolution webcam and Dolby Atmos-capable speakers. And it can run up to 17 hours on a single charge, which should easily get it through a workday of mixed use.

If you want a lightweight machine that looks and feels ready for hard work using Google’s vast suite of productivity apps and Gemini, this is a very reasonable option that can save you a few hundred bucks.

The Microsoft Surface Pro has been a stellar laptop-caliber tablet experience for a long time, and this year is no different. This Windows-powered slate is sleek, capable, and supremely versatile. Yes, you’ll need to buy a keyboard case to complete its transformation to a full-blown laptop, but I think it’s absolutely worth it to do so.

Getting the laptop option mentioned above requires spending more on a Surface Pro keyboard and Slim Pen 2 bundle, but the investment is well worth it. The essential accessories, along with the Pro’s adjustable viewing stand, are instrumental in giving it such commendable versatility.

Equipped with Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Series silicon, the Microsoft Surface Pro balances abundant power, stellar multitasking, and long battery life. We prefer the higher-end version, which features a stunning OLED screen. Lower-priced iterations use an IPS panel, down to a 12-inch display panel in the starter model.

You'll want a laptop that cuts through every task you throw at it while also lasting as long as you do. The selections below are packed with the latest processing and graphics technology to rise to the occasion.

If you travel frequently or commute with your computer, look for thin, light designs like the MacBook Air—the 13-inch model weighs in at just 2.7 pounds and the 15-inch at 3.3 pounds.

Gamers or content creators will want higher-end processors and graphics cards as well as bright, detailed screens. Students, and those who will spend most of their time logging into classes and watching the occasional movie or surfing the web, might want to consider a convertible laptop that also functions as a tablet.

With the latest laptops, battery life keeps improving. The reason newer laptops last longer without a bigger battery is because modern processors are getting more energy efficient. Today’s laptops will run between 8 and 20 hours on a single charge. Look for a battery that lasts at least 10 hours.

There are more than a dozen types of ports, including HDMI for video out and USB-C, which can be for almost anything with the right adapter, such as charging, but most users will only need a USB-C port. That’s because it’s possible to connect almost any type of peripheral to USB-C by itself or using an adapter.

If you don’t want to pack an adapter, consider a laptop with HDMI ports that can output video and audio from your laptop to a TV, monitor, or projector. They can support high-definition resolutions up to 4K and surround sound formats. Another handy option is an ethernet port, so you can connect your laptop to a wired network for faster and more reliable internet access.

The fastest processors on the market now offer blistering speeds and are great for gaming or video editing. But quicker speeds can sometimes make for a pricier laptop that has less battery life.

In laptop chips, Intel’s most popular lineup is its Core series, while Apple’s is its proprietary M-series processors (starting with the base M1). The middle ground in the Core and Ryzen lineups offers the best mix of performance and value. The most expensive laptops offer Intel Core i9 H-Series processors while midrange models tend to have Core i5 processors that offer a good balance between price and performance.

Screen quality is also crucial to a satisfying experience. Buy the best screen you can afford; your eyes will thank you later. Higher-resolution screens allow for greater image detail, though fonts on high-resolution displays can be small and difficult to read.

The most suitable screen size for most people ranges from 13 to 15 inches—the sweet spot between portability and enough real estate to get things done. The most common resolutions on laptops and 2-in-1 PCs currently hover just above 1920 x 1080 (also known as 1080p or Full HD). This keeps panel prices relatively low and fonts still large enough to view comfortably.

Pick a keyboard with a broad enough design and widely spaced keys if you’ll be doing a lot of typing. Also consider key travel (how far a key needs to be depressed until the keystroke is recognized), which can vary widely between models. Larger laptops tend to have better keyboards since the dimensions don't have to be downsized for smaller frames.

The more money you spend on your laptop, the longer you can expect it to last. In general, Macs have a reputation for lasting longer than Windows laptops. I have an eight-year-old MacBook Air that’s still going strong.

One factor to consider is that operating system updates that are released regularly tend to take up hard drive space, so if you buy a model with a larger drive, your laptop may last longer. To make the most of your laptop’s lifespan, keep the laptop clean, cool, updated, and backed up.

The weak spots of inexpensive laptops tend to be the keyboard, trackpad, and display. Manufacturers may skimp on these items hoping that potential buyers will focus more on processor speed. For starters, even if your funds are limited, look for a screen with at least Full HD (1920-by-1080) resolution.

It pays to be fussy when it comes to a laptop keyboard as that’s the component you’ll be interacting with the most. Buying a laptop with keyboard backlighting can help you see the keys better and avoid typing mistakes.

Some keyboards have adjustable brightness and color options for backlighting. Another important feature is a laptop keyboard with a full-size layout instead of a compact or tenkeyless layout without a numeric keypad.

#6391. How a Single Missing Atom Can Leave a Secret Fingerprint in Laser Light

Researchers have uncovered subtle optical signatures that could help distinguish atomic defects in a promising quantum material.

An atomic defect too small to see could leave a recognizable signature in laser light, giving scientists a new way to identify structures that may be useful for quantum technology. Researchers at the University at Buffalo have predicted how different atomic imperfections alter the optical behavior of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), a material made of boron and nitrogen atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern.

Using computer simulations, the team examined 10 types of defects, including missing boron or nitrogen atoms and sites where carbon atoms had taken their place. Some defects were predicted to dramatically increase the light produced at twice or even three times the frequency of an incoming laser. The strength of these signals depended on the light’s polarization, which describes the orientation of its electric field.

Even defects containing identical atoms can produce different optical responses if those atoms are arranged differently. When the researchers compared two configurations of four carbon atoms, they found that one was predicted to generate strong signals in two polarization directions, while the other produced a strong response in only one.

“These distinctive light responses could eventually allow us to experimentally identify not only which atoms are involved in a defect, but also precisely how they’re arranged,” says co-corresponding author Paras N. Prasad, SUNY Distinguished Professor, Samuel P. Capen Chair in the Department of Chemistry, and executive director of UB’s Institute for Lasers, Photonics, and Biophotonics (ILPB).

The findings, published October 19 in the American Chemical Society’s Nano Letters, could provide a reference for experimentally identifying atomic defects. By comparing measured light responses with the predicted optical fingerprints, researchers may eventually be able to determine which defects are present in a sample.

Some atomic defects in h-BN can emit single photons, individual particles of light released one at a time. These photons could transmit quantum information in future communication systems and support advanced sensing technologies. However, different defects have different properties, making accurate identification essential for finding useful sources of quantum light.

“Not all atomic defects are created equal. Making it easier to identify defects brings us another step closer to determining which ones have the properties we’re looking for,” says co-corresponding author Vasili Perebeinos, PhD, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the UB School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.

The simulations could help guide efforts to determine which defects generate quantum light and how to create them at specific locations within a material. Rather than relying on isolated photon emitters, the researchers ultimately hope to build organized arrays of precisely positioned defects.

“The ultimate goal is to create a material where we can precisely control the placement of defects that produce quantum light,” Perebeinos says. “Instead of relying on individual sources of quantum light, we want to create entire arrays of them that could be used in future quantum technologies. That’s the main motivation for studying defects in these materials.”

Reference: “Nonlinear Optical Fingerprints of Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride” by Olga Savkina, Davoud Adinehloo, Ivan Zhigulin, Pranati R. Kuntla, Viktor Labuntsov, Cecilia L. A. V. Campos, Alexander Baev, Andrey Kuzmin, Huamin Li, Igor Aharonovich, Paras N. Prasad and Vasili Perebeinos, 19 October 2026, Nano Letters. DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03684

The work was supported by the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research as part of the Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative (MURI). Support also came from the U.S. National Science Foundation, Australian Research Council, and the University at Buffalo Quantum Institute.

New research shows that a powerful 2021 marsquake emanating from Valles Marineris — the largest canyon in the solar system — was triggered by unexpected movement in a fault line deep below the gigantic structure, revealing that tectonic activity can still occur on geologically "dead" worlds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mars' supersize Valles Marineris — the largest known canyon in the solar system — is still tectonically active even though the Red Planet is geologically "dead," new research on a previously record-breaking marsquake reveals.

On Aug. 25, 2021, NASA's InSight lander, which touched down on the Red Planet in 2018, detected a powerful marsquake, designated S0976a. The Martian equivalent of an earthquake reached magnitude 4.2, which, at the time, was the most powerful quake that InSight or any other Mars lander had ever seen. (Since then, a 4.7 magnitude marsquake in May 2022 knocked it off the top spot, but S0976a remains second on this list.)

Unlike most marsquakes, which have been minor tremors triggered by meteorite impacts near InSight, S0976a was a deep rumble that originated from the opposite side of Mars as the robotic seismologist, in the western half of Valles Marineris.

In the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers reanalyzed the seismic wave data of S0976a and found that the quake originated from within a fault line running below the enormous canyon. The most likely explanation, they argue, is that there was tectonic movement in this hidden crustal crack.

"Valles Marineris is one of the most spectacular geological structures anywhere in the solar system, but until now we didn't know for certain that its faults are still active," study first author Jung-Hun Song, a researcher in the Department of Earth Science and Engineering at Imperial College London, said in a statement. "What we see is that this is not just a 'dead' fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased."

S0976a is the second-largest marsquake ever detected by NASA's InSight lander, shown here in a NASA clean room on April 30, 2015.

Valles Marineris is an enormous set of interconnected gullies and ravines stretching up to 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) in length, or roughly 10 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It is also up to 20 times wider and five times deeper, meaning that if you found yourself stranded at the bottom, it could take you a couple of months to climb out again.

The enormous chasm — named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft, which helped discover it in 1971 — is clearly visible from space, like a giant scar carved into the Red Planet's face. From orbit, you would also see the nearby Tharsis region, which is home to Mars' giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, which is at least three times taller than Mount Everest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

These imposing structures are proof that Mars was once geologically active, perhaps even more so than Earth. However, scientists think the Red Planet's surface has remained relatively unchanged for nearly 3 billion years, according to the European Space Agency.

Valles Marineris is almost as long as the continental U.S. is wide. (In this photo, captured by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter, an optical illusion known as relief inversion may make the canyon appear as if it is raised above the surface, which it is not.)

The reason for this is twofold. First, Mars is smaller than Earth, so its core and mantle have cooled much faster than our planet's and are, therefore, less dynamic. Second, Mars has no tectonic plates. Instead of giant patches of crust butting against each other, the Red Planet's outermost layer is almost completely intact and acts like a giant lid over its cooling molten innards. (Research published earlier this week throws the "dead" theory into question, hinting that magma may still lurk below dormant Martian volcanoes).

Despite this, Mars still has fault lines. But rather than being a boundary between tectonic plates, these lines are more like giant cracks in its crust, some of which are visible at the surface.

In the new study, researchers discovered proof of what they call a slip-strike marsquake, where "blocks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep, deeply rooted fault," the team said. They believe this occurred somewhere between 12 and 25 miles (20 to 40 km) below Valles Marineris.

The researchers also simulated several other potential causes of the marsquake, including a major asteroid strike or a landslide within the canyon, but nothing else could explain the patterns they saw.

Using seismic wave data captured by InSight, researchers were able to pinpoint the epicenter of the S0976a masquake (represented as a yellow star near the top of this map).

"What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction," Song said.

The finding also raises hopes that similar tectonic activity could one day be detected on other worlds across the solar system.

"Our study opens up exciting possibilities for discovering ongoing seismic activity on other planetary bodies that we might otherwise consider geologically inactive," Song said.

The discovery highlights the importance of detecting and studying marsquakes, which were only officially discovered in 2019, thanks to InSight. (Scientists have since uncovered older marsquakes, using data collected by the Viking landers in the late 1970s.)

InSight sent back a final selfie to Earth on Dec. 19, 2022, showing a heavy coating of Martian dust on its solar panels. Its mission was officially ended two days later.

"S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event," study co-author Doyeon Kim, head of Imperial College London's Terrestrial and Planetary Seismology Lab, said in the statement. "Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes."

Scientists have similarly used marsquake vibrations from InSight to map out Mars' interior, leading to several intriguing subsurface discoveries, including dozens of blobs left over from ancient protoplanets, the hidden cause of the planet's uneven hemispheres, a potentially active "mantle plume" and a gigantic underground water reservoir containing enough liquid to cover Mars with a mile-deep (1.6 km) ocean.

Unfortunately, in December 2022, InSight quite literally bit the dust: A thick covering of Martian powder blocked its solar panels, preventing the lander from returning signals to Earth and thus ending its mission.

This means we currently have no way of detecting new marsquakes. However, the new study proves that the lander's archived data can still lead to exciting discoveries.

Song, J., Kim, D., Kolawole, F., Davis, J. M., Parry, R., & Maguire, R. (2026). Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris. Nature Communications, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78193-6

#6387. Researchers Discover New Lace Bug Species on Japan’s Remote Ogasawara Islands

DNA uncovered a hidden species among Japan’s lace bugs and hints that a tree introduced by humans could help give rise to another.

Lace bugs living on two groups of Japan’s remote Ogasawara Islands had been classified as a single species, despite differences in their diets and coloring. Comparisons of their DNA have now revealed that they belong to two species, a distinction supported by subtle physical differences.

The archipelago lies roughly 900 to 1,000 kilometers (560 to 620 miles) south of Tokyo and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Its land snails and plants are celebrated for including species found nowhere else. About 440 insect species are also known to be unique to the islands, but their evolution has received far less attention.

Among those insects is Omoplax, a genus of lace bugs thought to have diversified rapidly across the islands. Jun Souma, of Hirosaki University’s Shirakami Research Center for Environmental Sciences, investigated these insects with Naoyuki Nakahama, of the Graduate School of Agriculture at Osaka Metropolitan University.

“The reason I took a particular interest in Omoplax desecta is that it feeds on both the native plant Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi and the introduced plant Calophyllum inophyllum in the Chichijima island group,” Souma said. “This is quite unusual for lace bugs, which typically exhibit high host specificity. I was also intrigued by the fact that it is distributed across multiple island groups, which is different from other Omoplax species.”

To investigate relationships among the insects, the researchers analyzed 52 specimens using MIG-seq, a method that provides DNA data from across the genome. Populations classified as Omoplax desecta on the Chichijima and Hahajima island groups were genetically distinct. The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys.

The genetic evidence helped explain differences Souma had noticed in the Hahajima insects.

“I had wondered why it fed exclusively on Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi and why there were no individuals with dark brown to black pronotum, which are sometimes seen in the Chichijima island group,” Souma explained. The pronotum is the plate just behind an insect’s head. “After conducting population genetic and phylogenetic analyses, I began to suspect that this population might be a distinct species. Upon closely observing their morphological characteristics, I was certain of this.”

Subtle differences in male genitalia confirmed the distinction. The Hahajima population is now described as Omoplax sandoru, named after the local name of its host plant.

For Omoplax desecta in the Chichijima group, the introduced tree offered another clue to how these insects might diversify. The DNA data indicate that its shift to feeding on Calophyllum inophyllum happened once, and recently. Whether that change will eventually produce another species remains a possibility rather than an established outcome.

“I also find it interesting that the introduction of Calophyllum inophyllum by humans may have led to a budding of future speciation in Omoplax desecta,” Souma added.

The researchers also reconstructed an evolutionary tree to trace relationships among the insects. That allowed them to test whether species with similar appearances and food preferences were one another’s closest relatives.

“The most surprising finding of my research was that species feeding on the same plant and appearing very similar are not necessarily sister groups,” said Souma, referring to groups that are each other’s closest evolutionary relatives. “Adaptive radiation among insects on oceanic islands may be more complex than comparisons of morphological characteristics and life histories would suggest at first glance.”

Adaptive radiation is the diversification of related organisms into species adapted to different ecological roles. Here, the findings point to both geographic isolation and shifts between host plants as drivers of species formation.

The researchers could not obtain DNA from two rare species, leaving gaps in the evolutionary picture. Further sampling will be needed to trace how these insects reached the islands and diversified.

Reference: “Genome-wide SNP data reveal phylogenetic relationships and further new species of lace bugs (Hemiptera, Heteroptera, Tingidae) endemic to the Japanese oceanic islands (the Ogasawara Islands), providing insight into their speciation” by Jun Souma and Naoyuki Nakahama, 8 October 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1294.205145

#6386. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6385. You Could Hire a Magician to Find Your Lost Stuff 400 Years Ago. The Real Danger Was If They Failed.

Service magicians known as “cunning folk” tracked down stolen goods with sieves and shears—until a spell went wrong.

Christabel Robyns was only trying to find some spoons and a pewter jug. In 1629, there were no smartphones or microchips to track lost items and no hidden cameras to play back video of how they vanished. Instead, Robyns, a widow, is thought to have turned to a more unusual way of getting her belongings back: magic. Word apparently got around, because she soon found herself accused of witchcraft and facing possible death by hanging.

Hers was hardly the only case of someone, especially a woman, being suspected of dabbling in the dark arts. In an age without modern technology, people with problems often turned to “cunning folk,” also known as service magicians, who used their own forms of magic to help. Some were healers or diviners. Others had a knack for finding lost or stolen objects. Whether Robyns was one of these cunning folk is unclear, but she must have either hired one or used magic herself, because she ended up before Ignatius Jurdain, a magistrate known for his rigid religious views. By then, courts across most of England had become skeptical of witchcraft accusations and were lenient toward the accused. Exeter retained its anti-witchcraft fanaticism.

That is where historian Mark Stoyle of the University of Southampton comes in. Stoyle was born and raised in Exeter and has long been fascinated by centuries-old accusations of the occult. His research shows that Robyns was saved when the chief justice of the Court of King’s Bench stepped in and sent her case to a higher court outside Exeter. She escaped with her life, but many others prosecuted on little more than hearsay weren’t as lucky. In Exeter, even service magicians, who were usually seen as harmless, were at risk, especially when their magic failed. That’s what happened to John Blachett in 1666, when a client hired him to find a lost hood. Blachett insisted the hood was in a neighbor’s house, but a search turned up nothing, and the client reported him. He was tried for “certain devilish and hateful arts” but, fortunately for him, wasn’t convicted.

“The city of Exeter possesses the grim distinction of being the last place in England in which people are known to have been executed for the crime of witchcraft,” Stoyle wrote in a study published in History: The Journal of the Historical Association. He also recently published the second edition of his book Witchcraft in Exeter, 1558–1666.

Executions for witchcraft in Exeter are traditionally said to have ended in 1685 with the hanging of Alice Molland. However, no record of her execution has been found, and Stoyle has argued that a court clerk may have misspelled her name, writing “Alicia” instead of “Avicia,” or Avis. Local archives record an Avis Molland who died in 1693, eight years after “Alice” was supposedly hanged. If Stoyle is right, England’s last executions for witchcraft took place three years earlier, in 1682. That year, Temperance Lloyd, Susanna Edwards and Mary Trembles, known as the “Bideford Witches,” were hanged at Heavitree, then a parish on the outskirts of Exeter. Sometimes simply being near a person considered suspicious was enough to seal someone’s fate. Long before germ theory, people who fell ill and died soon after meeting such a person were often thought to have been bewitched.

Society’s outcasts were frequent targets, too. Edwards, Lloyd, and Trembles were poor, living on parish relief and whatever scraps they could find. Each was also unmarried, widowed or abandoned, and a woman living alone was already viewed with suspicion. If someone fell ill with smallpox after meeting or even passing such a woman, she could end up in a prison cell awaiting a trial that might end in a death sentence. Female cunning folk faced particular danger in Exeter, because their work was easily mistaken for witchcraft. In 1642, a client hired Anne King, a weaver’s wife, to find out who had stolen a purse. King balanced a sieve on a pair of shears and recited suspects’ names, and the sieve turned when she said the name Marie Matthews. King herself was then reported and arrested for witchcraft, but she was released on bail and survived.

In most of England, cunning folk went about their business while the authorities looked the other way. Stoyle’s research in the archives, however, shows that they often met a hostile reception in Exeter, where the outcomes for accused witches were sometimes recorded in court documents. A conviction was marked “culpabilis,” meaning “guilty,” followed by “susp.,” short for the Latin “suspensus,” meaning “hanged.” Burial records sometimes confirm these executions. One such case was Thomasin Short, whose name appears with several different spellings. She had been arrested again and again as a “scold,” an unruly woman who constantly criticized others and picked fights. Short is said to have shouted a dark threat at a family that then suffered several deaths. She was found guilty of witchcraft, and her court record is marked “susp.”

“The particular sets of circumstances which resulted in Shorte…being hanged when a number of other supposed Exeter witches managed to escape that fate can only be guessed at,” said Stoyle. He suspects that an outburst of “popular rage,” combined with what seemed to be unimpeachable evidence, “...eventually persuaded the judges to hand down a death sentence.”

Today, finding a lost spoon takes nothing more than a look under the couch cushions, but in 17th-century Exeter, searching the wrong way could cost a woman her life.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their stars' glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6382. Amazon’s New Kindle Paperwhite Is Here. Here’s What’s Different From the Last Version.

From slimmer designs to updated displays and charging features, here's what's changed with Amazon's latest e-readers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon has refreshed its Kindle lineup for 2026, introducing new versions of the popular Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition. Both e-readers have notable design updates, but if you already own a previous model, you might wonder whether it's worth upgrading.

The short answer? It depends on which Kindle you're using. Compared to the 2024 models, the latest Paperwhites offer a sleeker design, updated display technology, and some welcome improvements to everyday usability. The Signature Edition, in particular, gets a few extras that make it feel more like a premium device. Here's what's changed and what's stayed the same.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition

The most noticeable upgrade is the design and appearance. Amazon has made the standard Paperwhite thinner and slightly lighter, reducing its thickness from 7.8 millimeters to 6.8 millimeters. It also weighs approximately 204 grams, compared to the previous model's 211 grams. That might not sound like much, but a slimmer e-reader is always welcome when you're holding it for hours or slipping it into a bag.

The redesigned display construction also creates a more seamless, edge-to-edge look. Amazon uses a new display stack with an oxide thin-film transistor backplane, designed to deliver excellent contrast, deeper blacks, and crisp text. The screen is still 7 inches with a 300-ppi resolution, so don't expect a dramatic jump in sharpness over the 2024 model.

Another small but genuinely useful change is the power button's placement. Instead of sitting along the bottom edge, where it was easy to press accidentally, it's now positioned on the upper-right side.

And if battery life is your biggest concern, there's good news: Amazon still promises up to 12 weeks on a single charge, just like the previous generation. The new model also maintains its IPX8 waterproof rating and adjustable warm lighting.

The Signature Edition receives the same thinner design and updated screen construction, but Amazon has made a few additional changes to distinguish it from the standard Paperwhite.

For starters, it now has an aluminum back instead of the previous model's plastic construction, giving it a more premium look and feel. That upgrade comes with a trade-off, though: At approximately 229 grams, the new Signature Edition is actually a little heavier than its 214-gram predecessor.

The new model also introduces pogo-pin connectors for charging and accessories. These let the Kindle connect to Amazon's new charging stand and a magnetic Page-Turn Cover with physical buttons, which could appeal to readers who miss the page-turn buttons on older e-readers.

One important difference is that the 2024 Signature Edition supported conventional Qi wireless charging, while the 2026 model switches to the new contact-based pogo-pin system.

Amazon also highlights a double-tap feature that lets you advance pages by tapping the side or back of the device, making one-handed reading a little easier.

Otherwise, you'll still get 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. Both generations are waterproof, too.

If you're shopping for a new Kindle rather than replacing an older one, the decision mostly comes down to whether the Signature Edition's premium features are worth an additional $50.

The standard Paperwhite starts at $199.99 and includes 16GB of storage, adjustable warm lighting, and a 7-inch glare-free display.

For $249.99, the Signature Edition doubles the storage to 32GB, adds an aluminum back and automatic brightness adjustment, and supports the new pogo-pin charging accessories. It's also available in Seaglass Green, whereas the regular Paperwhite comes in Graphite.

Both deliver essentially the same core reading experience, so casual readers probably won't miss much by sticking with the less expensive version.

If you already own a 2024 Kindle Paperwhite or Signature Edition and it's working perfectly fine, you probably don't need to replace it. You're still getting the same screen size and resolution, excellent battery life, waterproofing, and access to Amazon's massive Kindle library.

However, if you're upgrading from an older 2021 Paperwhite—or you're shopping for your first e-reader—the 2026 models are worth considering. The thinner design, improved screen construction, and updated controls make the latest lineup more appealing.

For most readers, the regular Paperwhite will be more than enough. But if you read every day, want the premium aluminum design, or like the idea of a case with physical page-turn buttons, the Signature Edition is a worthwhile step up.

A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.
